claims.text: The target material is a disordered, multi-principal-element refractory high-entropy alloy.
The target refractory HEA has significant lattice distortion.
The target refractory HEA has nanoscale heterogeneous grain-boundary structures.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases activation barriers for dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion acts together with nanoscale grain-boundary heterogeneity to stabilize edge dislocations.
The combined structural features preferentially favor edge-dislocation mobility over conventional screw-dislocation mechanisms.
Edge dislocations govern elevated-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory BCC HEAs.
Edge-dislocation stabilization governs the distinctive thermoelastic response of refractory HEAs.
A higher-distortion HEA will retain greater yield strength at elevated temperature than a similar lower-distortion alloy.
The higher-distortion HEA will display more dominant edge-dislocation activity than the lower-distortion baseline.
The higher-distortion HEA will have a modified and possibly less temperature-sensitive elastic modulus than the lower-distortion baseline.
A single-phase refractory HEA can remain stable throughout the proposed 300°C to 800°C testing range.
The proposed tests cover approximately 300°C to 800°C under static and dynamic loading.
Minimizing elemental size mismatch will reduce lattice distortion in the baseline alloy.
Increasing compositional complexity will intentionally produce the high-distortion sample.
In situ neutron diffraction and electron microscopy can identify the operative edge-versus-screw dislocation character in refractory HEAs.
Holding the overall composition and initial microstructure comparable while changing lattice distortion will reveal whether lattice distortion is the governing cause.
Failure to observe enhanced strength, a distinct thermoelastic response, or dominant edge-dislocation activity in the higher-distortion sample would falsify the hypothesis.
